section_summary: This section contains diplomatic correspondence, consular despatches, memoranda, and telegrams from 1930 to 1939 relating to Japanese Emperor Hirohito, focused primarily on the annual exchange of official birthday greetings between President Franklin D. Roosevelt and the Emperor. It also documents diplomatic sensitivities and friction over American press depictions of the Emperor, including Japanese objections to a feature in Life magazine and efforts by the Japanese Consul General in Singapore to suppress copies of Ken magazine containing an objectionable caricature. In addition, the section includes reports on anti-foreign ideology ('Sonno Joi') promoted in Japanese-ruled Korea, extensive celebrations and economic appeals by the Japanese community in Peru on the Emperor's 37th birthday, and consular courtesies exchanged in Sumatra in 1930.

subfiles.about: A Special Agent reports on an anti-Japanese rally and demonstration in New York organized by the American Friends of the Chinese People.
subfiles.from: Special Agent in Charge
keywords: American Friends of the Chinese People
subfiles.summary: This final page of an investigative report details proceedings connected with an anti-war meeting in New York City. A resolution urging the American public to take measures against Japanese aggressions in China was delivered by the American Friends of the Chinese People to the Japanese Consulate at 500 Fifth Avenue on September 18, 1936, accompanied by picketing. A message of support was also voted to be cabled to the commanding officer of the Chinese 19th Route Army. The report concludes with remarks by Joseph Freeman, editor of New Masses, who denounced Hitler, Mussolini, and William Randolph Hearst, asserting that the Emperor of Japan was collaborating with European fascists in creating wars.
subfiles.title: Report on Meeting of American Friends of the Chinese People and Anti-Japanese Protest
subfiles.to: Department of State

subfiles.about: Vice Consul Ralph Cory transmits and critiques an editorial from the government-subsidized Keijo Nippo promoting a modernized 'Sonno Joi' movement in Chosen.
subfiles.from: Ralph Cory, American Vice Consul, Seoul
subfiles.summary: Vice Consul Ralph Cory forwards to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo an English translation of an editorial from the December 30, 1936, edition of Keijo Nippo, a Japanese daily subsidized by the Government General of Chosen. Cory observes that the editorial provides further evidence of officially encouraged xenophobia in Korea, using strained historical analogies that categorize democracy, Marxism, and liberalism as mental diseases afflicting Japan after World War I. The editorial argues that international rivalries are increasingly fought over opposing ideologies rather than military weapons, citing the Japanese-German Anti-Comintern Pact as an example. It urges reviving the Meiji Restoration concept of 'Reverence for the Emperor and Expulsion of Foreigners' (Sonno Joi) to purify the national spirit and combat foreign ideas in Chosen.
subfiles.title: Despatch Transmitting Translation of Keijo Nippo Editorial 'Reverence for the Emperor and Expulsion of Foreigners in a New Form'
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo

subfiles.about: President Franklin D. Roosevelt extends official birthday greetings and best wishes to Emperor Hirohito.
subfiles.from: Franklin D. Roosevelt, President of the United States
subfiles.summary: President Franklin D. Roosevelt sends a formal telegram from the White House to the Emperor of Japan on April 29, 1937. The President extends his sincere greetings and best wishes for the Emperor's continued health and happiness upon the anniversary of his birth. The message represents the annual diplomatic birthday felicitation sent by the American head of state.
subfiles.title: Telegram from President Roosevelt to the Emperor of Japan on His Birthday
subfiles.to: Hirohito, Emperor of Japan

subfiles.about: Emperor Hirohito expresses thanks to President Roosevelt for birthday congratulations, referred to the State Department by Stephen Early.
subfiles.from: Hirohito, Emperor of Japan
subfiles.summary: Emperor Hirohito telegraphs President Franklin D. Roosevelt from Tokyo to express his sincere thanks and appreciation for the President's courteous message of congratulations and good wishes on his birthday. The telegram, received in Washington via RCA on April 30, 1937, was referred to the Department of State by Assistant Secretary to the President Stephen Early. The document includes Early's referral slip dated April 30, 1937.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Emperor Hirohito to President Roosevelt Acknowledging Birthday Greetings (with White House Referral Slip)
subfiles.to: Franklin D. Roosevelt, President of the United States

subfiles.about: The Secretary of State informs Ambassador Grew of the text of President Roosevelt's birthday telegram to the Emperor of Japan.
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull, Secretary of State
subfiles.summary: The Department of State sends Instruction No. 1247 to American Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo for the Embassy's information. The message quotes the full text of President Roosevelt's April 29, 1937, birthday telegram to Emperor Hirohito extending greetings and wishes for health and happiness. The instruction was drafted in the Division of Protocol and approved by Far Eastern Affairs.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 1247 to the American Ambassador at Tokyo Quoting President's Birthday Greeting
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo

subfiles.about: Assistant Secretary Hugh R. Wilson reports on Japanese Counselor Suma's visit regarding an objectionable article on the Emperor in Life magazine.
subfiles.from: Hugh R. Wilson, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.summary: Assistant Secretary of State Hugh R. Wilson reports to Secretary of State Cordell Hull regarding a morning call by Yakichiro Suma, Counselor of the Japanese Embassy. Suma presented a copy of the December 6, 1937, issue of Life magazine containing pictures and an article concerning the Emperor of Japan that deeply offended Japanese sensibilities. Wilson expressed spontaneous personal regret that the article had been printed, and Suma stated that if the Secretary of State made a similar spontaneous statement, the incident would be closed without further publicity. Wilson reminded Suma that the United States government has no control over the press, but agreed to bring the matter to Secretary Hull's attention.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Hugh R. Wilson on Japanese Embassy Complaint Concerning Life Magazine Article
subfiles.to: Cordell Hull, Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Adviser James Clement Dunn reports that Secretary Hull's expression of regret regarding the Life magazine article was telephoned to Counselor Suma.
subfiles.from: James Clement Dunn, Adviser on Political Relations
subfiles.summary: James Clement Dunn, Adviser on Political Relations, writes to Assistant Secretary Hugh R. Wilson regarding Wilson's memorandum of December 4. Dunn brought the matter to the attention of Secretary Hull, who instructed him to inform Japanese Counselor Yakichiro Suma that he was very sorry indeed that an article of this kind had been published. Dunn telephoned this message to Suma on the afternoon of December 4, 1937, and Suma expressed his sincere gratitude for the statement.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by James Clement Dunn on Communicating Regret to Japanese Counselor Suma
subfiles.to: Hugh R. Wilson, Assistant Secretary of State

subfiles.about: A White House referral slip forwarding correspondence to Chief of Protocol George T. Summerlin for attention.
subfiles.from: Stephen Early, Secretary to the President
subfiles.summary: Stephen Early, Secretary to the President, refers a White House communication to George T. Summerlin of the State Department for official attention. The referral slip is dated May 1, 1939, and bears stamps from the Division of Far Eastern Affairs. It is filed in the volume out of chronological sequence, preceding April 1938 records.
subfiles.title: White House Referral Slip to George T. Summerlin
subfiles.to: George T. Summerlin, Department of State

subfiles.about: Consul Thomas McEnelly reports on the Japanese Consul General's attempts to buy up an issue of 'Ken' magazine caricaturing the Emperor and details his controversial conduct in Singapore.
subfiles.from: Thomas McEnelly, American Consul, Singapore
subfiles.summary: American Consul Thomas McEnelly in Singapore submits Despatch No. 418 reporting that Japanese Consul General I. Okamoto visited the Consulate General after receiving cable instructions from Tokyo to buy up all copies of the April 1938 debut issue of the American magazine 'Ken'. The magazine contained an objectionable cartoon entitled 'Plagues' depicting Emperor Hirohito alongside Hitler, Mussolini, and Franco. Okamoto noted that while serving as Consul in Seattle, he had previously initiated a diplomatic protest over an American cartoon of the Emperor. McEnelly also reports on Okamoto's contentious local behavior, including bringing uninvited Japanese players to the British-controlled Singapore Golf Club and demanding honorary consular membership, as well as reports from British military intelligence head Lt. Col. Hayley-Bell that Okamoto had attempted to bribe Singapore newspaper editors with costly Japanese gifts. The despatch is preserved in the file in multiple copies, including ordinary mail and air mail versions.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 418 on Objectionable Cartoon of Japanese Emperor in Ken Magazine and Activities of Consul General Okamoto
subfiles.to: Cordell Hull, Secretary of State

subfiles.about: The Division of Protocol consults the Division of Far Eastern Affairs on the text of the President's annual birthday message to the Emperor of Japan.
subfiles.from: H. Charles Spruks, Division of Protocol
subfiles.summary: H. Charles Spruks of the Division of Protocol sends an internal memorandum to Maxwell M. Hamilton, Chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, regarding the upcoming birthday of the Emperor of Japan on April 29, 1938. Spruks attaches the congratulatory telegram sent by the President the previous year and asks whether a similar routine message should be sent or if Far Eastern Affairs preferred drafting a special message. The inquiry reflects standard departmental coordination to ensure head-of-state messages conformed to prevailing diplomatic policy.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by H. Charles Spruks regarding Birthday Message to the Emperor of Japan
subfiles.to: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: President Roosevelt sends birthday felicitations and wishes for health and well-being to the Emperor of Japan.
subfiles.from: Franklin D. Roosevelt, President of the United States
subfiles.summary: President Franklin D. Roosevelt sends a formal telegram from the White House to the Emperor of Japan in Tokyo on April 29, 1938. The President extends his sincere felicitations upon the occasion of the Emperor's birthday and best wishes for continued health and well-being. The text was prepared by the Division of Protocol and approved by Far Eastern Affairs.
subfiles.title: Telegram from President Roosevelt to the Emperor of Japan on His Birthday
subfiles.to: Hirohito, Emperor of Japan

subfiles.about: Emperor Hirohito thanks President Roosevelt for his birthday message, referred to the State Department by M. H. McIntyre.
subfiles.from: Hirohito, Emperor of Japan
subfiles.summary: Emperor Hirohito cables President Franklin D. Roosevelt from Tokyo to express his sincere thanks for the President's courteous message of congratulation and good wishes on his birthday. The telegram, received via RCA in Washington on April 30, 1938, was forwarded to the State Department by Secretary to the President M. H. McIntyre. The document includes McIntyre's White House referral slip dated April 30, 1938.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Emperor Hirohito to President Roosevelt Acknowledging Birthday Greetings (with White House Referral Slip)
subfiles.to: Franklin D. Roosevelt, President of the United States

subfiles.about: The Secretary of State transmits the text of the President's birthday greeting to the Emperor of Japan to Ambassador Grew in Tokyo.
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull, Secretary of State
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Cordell Hull issues Instruction No. 1481 to American Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo, quoting for his information the text of President Roosevelt's birthday telegram sent to Emperor Hirohito on April 29, 1938. The instruction provided the Embassy with the exact wording of the head-of-state exchange. It was prepared in the Division of Protocol and initialed by Far Eastern Affairs.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 1481 to the American Ambassador at Tokyo Quoting President's Birthday Greeting
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo

subfiles.about: Consul General Homer Brett reports on celebrations of the Emperor's birthday by the Japanese colony in Peru, including appeals on civic loyalty and textile import quotas.
subfiles.from: Homer Brett, American Consul General, Callao-Lima, Peru
subfiles.summary: Consul General Homer Brett submits an extensive voluntary political report describing celebrations in Peru on April 29, 1938, commemorating the 37th birthday of Emperor Hirohito. The report includes full translations of prominent articles and advertisements published in Lima newspapers such as El Comercio and La Prensa. In an address entitled 'To Our Peruvian Friends', Sadajiro Yumoto, President of the Central Japanese Society of Peru, emphasizes traditional Japanese loyalty, cites the 1890 Imperial Rescript on Education of Emperor Meiji, and argues that Peruvian-born children of Japanese parents are loyal Peruvian citizens, though Brett notes Peruvian authorities refuse to recognize them as such or permit them to serve in the Peruvian military. The report also translates a detailed commercial study by R. Takahashi, President of the Japanese Association of Commerce and Industry, who presents Japanese foreign trade statistics for 1936 and 1937 and argues for the abolition of Peruvian quotas on Japanese cotton textiles. Brett concludes that Peruvian cotton manufacturers and authorities remain strongly committed to maintaining import quotas against Japanese competition.
subfiles.title: Voluntary Political Report: Celebration of Japanese Emperor's Birthday in Peru
subfiles.to: Cordell Hull, Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Spruks notes that the Division of Far Eastern Affairs preferred the drafted text for the Emperor of Japan's birthday telegram.
subfiles.from: H. Charles Spruks, Division of Protocol
subfiles.summary: H. Charles Spruks of the Division of Protocol files an internal memorandum regarding the draft telegram to the Emperor of Japan on his birthday. Spruks notes that although the attached telegram was quite similar to the one sent in 1937, the Division of Far Eastern Affairs preferred the telegram as drafted. The memorandum documents inter-office agreement on the precise wording of the message.
subfiles.title: Memorandum for File by H. Charles Spruks regarding Birthday Telegram to the Emperor of Japan
subfiles.to: File

subfiles.about: President Roosevelt extends cordial birthday greetings and good wishes for personal welfare to Emperor Hirohito.
subfiles.from: Franklin D. Roosevelt, President of the United States
subfiles.summary: President Franklin D. Roosevelt sends a telegram from the White House to Emperor Hirohito in Tokyo on April 29, 1939. The President extends cordial greetings and good wishes for the Emperor's personal welfare upon the anniversary of his birth. The telegram was prepared in the Division of Protocol and approved by Far Eastern Affairs.
subfiles.title: Telegram from President Roosevelt to Emperor Hirohito on His Birthday
subfiles.to: Hirohito, Emperor of Japan

subfiles.about: The Secretary of State transmits to Ambassador Grew the text of the President's birthday greeting to Emperor Hirohito.
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull, Secretary of State
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Cordell Hull sends Instruction No. 1719 to American Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo quoting the text of President Roosevelt's birthday telegram sent to Emperor Hirohito on April 29, 1939. The quoted message extends cordial greetings and good wishes on the anniversary of the Emperor's birth. The instruction provided the Tokyo Embassy with the official diplomatic record.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 1719 to the American Ambassador at Tokyo Quoting President's Birthday Greeting
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo

subfiles.about: Department of State file copy of President Roosevelt's birthday telegram to Emperor Hirohito.
subfiles.from: Franklin D. Roosevelt, President of the United States
subfiles.summary: This document is an official file copy of President Franklin D. Roosevelt's telegram sent from the White House to Emperor Hirohito in Tokyo on April 29, 1939. It extends cordial greetings and good wishes upon the anniversary of the Emperor's birth. The text corresponds to the finalized version without the supplementary phrase 'for your personal welfare', stamped as received in Far Eastern Affairs on May 5, 1939.
subfiles.title: Telegram (File Copy) from President Roosevelt to Emperor Hirohito on His Birthday
subfiles.to: Hirohito, Emperor of Japan

subfiles.about: Acting Consul Daniel M. Braddock informs Japanese Consul T. Suwa that the U.S. flag is being flown in honor of the Emperor's birthday.
subfiles.from: Daniel M. Braddock, Acting Consul of the United States of America, Medan
subfiles.summary: Daniel M. Braddock, Acting American Consul in Medan, Sumatra, writes to Japanese Consul T. Suwa on April 29, 1930. Braddock informs Suwa that the flag of the United States is being flown at the Consulate in honor of the birthday of His Imperial Majesty the Emperor of Japan. Braddock takes the occasion to wish the Emperor a long and prosperous reign and extends assurances of high consideration. A copy was transmitted to the Department of State and filed under decimal classification 894.001H61 in June 1930.
subfiles.title: Letter from Acting Consul Daniel M. Braddock to Japanese Consul T. Suwa on the Emperor's Birthday
subfiles.to: T. Suwa, Consul of Japan, Medan, Sumatra

subfiles.about: Japanese Consul T. Suwa acknowledges and thanks Acting Consul Braddock for flying the U.S. flag in honor of the Emperor's birthday.
subfiles.from: T. Suwa, Consul for Japan, Medan
subfiles.summary: T. Suwa, Consul for Japan at Medan, Sumatra, writes on April 29, 1930, to acknowledge receipt of a letter of even date from American Acting Consul Daniel M. Braddock. Suwa expresses his sincere thanks for Braddock's courtesy in flying the United States flag in honor of the birthday of His Imperial Majesty the Emperor of Japan. Suwa also conveys gratitude for Braddock's wishes for a long and prosperous reign for the Emperor. A certified copy was retained for the files of the Department of State.
subfiles.title: Letter from Japanese Consul T. Suwa to Acting Consul Daniel M. Braddock Acknowledging Birthday Greetings
subfiles.to: Daniel M. Braddock, Acting Consul for the United States of America, Medan
